confirmed.sentence: Better-looking video does not fix this, because the visual quality of a world model does not reliably predict whether policies succeed in it [5].
confirmed.issue: The sentence says [5] studied policies that succeed inside the world model, meaning the world model serves as the environment where a policy is trained or evaluated. World-in-World does something different. The world model is a planning aid: a proposal policy suggests candidate plans, the world model imagines rollouts, and a revision policy picks one. That plan is then carried out in the real environment (Habitat-Sim or CoppeliaSim), and task success is measured there. So the finding is that visual quality does not guarantee the task success of agents that plan with the world model. It is not about success inside the world model. In content/05-justification.md this misreading matters, because the paragraph describes policies trained inside the world model.
confirmed.evidence: Abstract: "visual quality alone does not guarantee task success, controllability matters more". Sec. 2 / Fig. 3: "The world model then predicts the corresponding future states... The revision policy evaluates all rollouts and commits to the best, yielding decision. This decision is applied in the environment, closing the interaction loop." Sec. 2.1: "the agent executes the top-scoring plan in the environment".
confirmed.fix_en: Better-looking video does not fix this, because the visual quality of a world model does not reliably predict whether agents that plan with it succeed at their tasks [5].
confirmed.fix_pl: Lepiej wyglądające wideo tego nie naprawia, ponieważ jakość wizualna modelu świata nie pozwala wiarygodnie przewidzieć, czy agenci planujący z jego pomocą odnoszą sukces w zadaniach [5].

votes.reason:
The problem is real and I could not refute it. In both languages "succeed in it" / "odnoszą w nim sukces" means success inside the world model. The paragraph in content/05-justification.md (and PL line 43) is about policies trained inside the world model, which pushes the reader toward that reading.

What the paper does (arXiv 2510.18135, Zhang et al.): the world model is not the place where policies are trained or scored. It is used for online planning. A proposal policy suggests plans, the world model imagines the rollouts, a revision policy picks the best one, and that plan is then executed in the real simulator environment, where task success is measured. The abstract asks "do WMs actually help agents succeed at embodied tasks?" and concludes that visual quality alone does not guarantee task success. So the finding is about agents that plan with the world model and act in the environment. It is not about success inside the model.

The proposed EN fix says exactly that. It is minimal, and it is no stronger than the paper, since "does not reliably predict" fits "does not guarantee". The PL fix is natural Polish and matches the EN fix. Both follow the style rules: first person, no semicolons, no dashes, no numbers, no "sim".

The corrected sentence is also consistent with the plan's related-work paragraph on [5] (PL line 57), which already describes the result correctly.

It adds nothing new and does not strengthen the claim. "Does not reliably predict" is a fair paraphrase of "does not necessarily translate". confirmed.sentence: LeCun [7] argues that it should predict the representation of the future observation rather than its pixels, so that it can drop unpredictable detail such as texture or sensor noise.
confirmed.issue: The main claim is supported: JEPA predicts in representation space and the encoder can drop irrelevant or unpredictable detail. Texture is LeCun's own example. Sensor noise is not. The paper never uses it as an example of unpredictable detail, and the only mention of noise is about denoising autoencoders. The examples he actually gives are the texture of a carpet, leaves of a tree moving in the wind, ripples on a pond, and the texture of the sidewalk.
confirmed.evidence: Section 4.4 (p. 27): "it is essentially impossible to predict every pixel value of every future frame. The details of the texture on a carpet, the leaves of a tree moving in the wind, or the ripples on a pond, cannot be predicted accurately". p. 24: "ignoring irrelevant details such as the trees bordering the road or the texture of the sidewalk". A search of the full text finds no 'sensor noise'.

votes.reason: I tried to refute the claim and could not. I searched the full text of LeCun (2022), v0.9.2 (scratchpad l3.txt), for "noise", "noisy" and "sensor". "Sensor noise" never appears as an example of unpredictable detail. "Noisy" only turns up for noisy latent variables and autoencoders (VAE, noisy AE by Doi et al.) and in the appendix on denoising autoencoders. "Sensors" only turns up in the perception module, in the list of uncertainty types (sensors that give partial information, which is epistemic uncertainty and not noise) and in the list of data regimes. So the main claim holds. JEPA predicts in representation space, and its encoders can drop unpredictable or irrelevant detail (p. 24: "eschewing the need to predict every detail of y ... irrelevant details have been eliminated"; p. 27-28: "Unpredictable details will be eliminated by the invariance properties of the encoder"). Texture is his own example (p. 24: "texture of the sidewalk"; p. 27: "texture on a carpet"). The "such as" examples are presented as LeCun's, so "sensor noise" puts an example in his mouth that he never gives. It is a small problem, but it is real. The proposed fix is accurate. p. 27 says "the leaves of a tree moving in the wind ... cannot be predicted accurately", and p. 4 lists "tree leaves in the wind" among things that behave in unpredictable ways. The fix is also minimal, does not strengthen the claim and follows the style rules. The PL fix says the same thing as the EN fix, and "liście poruszane wiatrem" is natural Polish. votes.reason: This is a real but minor problem. I checked the arXiv 2605.06388 abstract ("Reconstruction or Semantics? What Makes a Latent Space Useful for Robotic World Models", Nilaksh, Jha, Zholus, Chandar). Most of the plan's sentence is correct: the paper compares six reconstruction and semantic encoders on BridgeV2, and planning and downstream policy performance is one of its three evaluation axes. The problem is that the source hedges its main claim. It says semantic encoders (V-JEPA 2.1, Web-DINO, SigLIP 2) "generally excel across the other two axes", and it also says reconstruction encoders (VAE, Cosmos) do well on pixel-level fidelity. The plan's flat "were better" drops that hedge, so it reads as a slightly stronger claim than the paper makes. The round 5 citation notes (research/verification-loop-citations.md line 246) saw the dropped "generally" and accepted it as fine for a one-line summary. That makes this a borderline call. I still count it as real because it is about matching the source, not about style: adding back the source's own word is the smallest possible change and does not strengthen the claim. The proposed EN fix is correct. The PL fix is natural Polish and says the same thing as the EN fix.

In content/09-methods.md:11, the EN phrase "with jobs managed by SLURM" applies to the whole clause, so it covers both the WCSS H100 nodes and PLGrid. In output/IPB_Grzegorz_Piotrowski_PL.md:99, "oraz na zasobach PLGrid, gdzie zadaniami zarządza SLURM" ties SLURM only to PLGrid, which suggests WCSS might not use SLURM. That suggestion is wrong.
